BEGINNER1. What Makes a File a Module?

Definition

In TypeScript (as in modern JavaScript), any file containing a top-level import or export is treated as a module — its declarations are scoped to that file rather than shared globally.

Real-world analogy: A module is like a sealed room — nothing inside is visible from outside unless you explicitly hand it through the door (export), and you can only bring things in through the door too (import). 
// math.ts - has an export, so it's a module
export function add(a: number, b: number): number {
    return a + b;
}

// A file with no import/export is a "script" - its declarations
// are global and visible to every other script in the project
💡 Tip: If a file genuinely has nothing to import or export but you still want it scoped as a module, add export {}; at the top — a common fix for "duplicate declaration" errors in standalone .ts files.

BEGINNER2. Named Exports and Imports

// utils.ts
export const PI = 3.14159;

export function double(n: number): number {
    return n * 2;
}

export interface Point {
    x: number;
    y: number;
}
// main.ts
import { PI, double, Point } from "./utils";

const p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2 };
console.log(double(PI));   // 6.28318

Renaming on Import/Export with as

// utils.ts
export { double as multiplyByTwo };

// main.ts
import { multiplyByTwo as timesTwo } from "./utils";
console.log(timesTwo(5));   // 10

Importing Everything as a Namespace Object

import * as MathUtils from "./utils";

console.log(MathUtils.PI);
console.log(MathUtils.double(4));

BEGINNER3. Default Exports

// logger.ts
export default class Logger {
    log(message: string): void {
        console.log(`[LOG] ${message}`);
    }
}
// main.ts
import Logger from "./logger";   // no curly braces - default import can be named anything

const logger = new Logger();
logger.log("App started");

Default Export of a Function

// greet.ts
export default function greet(name: string): string {
    return `Hello, ${name}`;
}

// main.ts
import greet from "./greet";
console.log(greet("Sam"));
⚠️ Common Pitfall: A module can only have one default export but any number of named exports. Mixing conventions inconsistently across a codebase makes imports harder to predict — pick one style and stick with it (see Best Practices).

INTERMEDIATE4. Re-exporting and Barrel Files

A "barrel" file re-exports everything from several modules through one entry point, simplifying imports elsewhere in the app.

// components/Button.ts
export interface ButtonProps { label: string; }
export function Button(props: ButtonProps) { /* ... */ }

// components/Input.ts
export interface InputProps { placeholder: string; }
export function Input(props: InputProps) { /* ... */ }

// components/index.ts (the barrel file)
export * from "./Button";
export * from "./Input";
// main.ts - one import instead of two
import { Button, Input, ButtonProps, InputProps } from "./components";

Re-exporting with Renaming

// index.ts
export { Button as PrimaryButton } from "./Button";

INTERMEDIATE5. Type-Only Imports and Exports

Since TypeScript 3.8, you can mark an import or export as type-only, guaranteeing it's completely erased from the compiled JavaScript output.

// types.ts
export interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
}

// main.ts
import type { User } from "./types";
// or mix value and type imports:
import { someFunction, type User as UserType } from "./mixed";

const user: User = { id: 1, name: "Nico" };
Why it matters: Build tools that compile files independently (like esbuild or ts-jest with isolatedModules) can't always tell whether an import is a type or a value. import type removes the ambiguity and guarantees no runtime import is emitted for something that's purely a type.

INTERMEDIATE6. Dynamic import()

The dynamic import() function loads a module asynchronously at runtime, returning a Promise — useful for code splitting and lazy loading.

async function loadChart() {
    const { renderChart } = await import("./chart");
    renderChart();
}

// Typing the resolved module
async function loadUtils() {
    const utils = await import("./utils");
    console.log(utils.PI);   // fully typed, same as a static import
}
💡 Tip: Dynamic import() is commonly used for route-based code splitting in frameworks like React (React.lazy(() => import("./Page"))) so large bundles only load when actually needed.

ADVANCED7. Declaration Files (.d.ts)

A .d.ts file contains only type information — no runtime code — describing the shape of JavaScript that TypeScript otherwise couldn't understand, such as an untyped npm package.

// legacy-lib.d.ts
declare module "legacy-lib" {
    export function formatCurrency(amount: number): string;
    export const VERSION: string;
}
// main.ts
import { formatCurrency, VERSION } from "legacy-lib";
console.log(formatCurrency(1000));   // fully type-checked, even though
                                       // legacy-lib itself is plain JS

Global Ambient Declarations

// globals.d.ts
declare const APP_VERSION: string;   // e.g. injected by a bundler at build time

console.log(APP_VERSION);   // usable anywhere, no import needed
💡 Tip: Many popular packages ship their own .d.ts files, or the community maintains them separately under @types/package-name (the DefinitelyTyped project) — install with npm i -D @types/package-name.

ADVANCED8. Namespaces

Namespaces predate ES modules and provide a way to group related code under a single named object, generating actual runtime code (unlike modules, which use the file system as the boundary).

namespace Validation {
    export interface StringValidator {
        isValid(s: string): boolean;
    }

    export class EmailValidator implements StringValidator {
        isValid(s: string): boolean {
            return /^[^@]+@[^@]+\.[^@]+$/.test(s);
        }
    }
}

const validator = new Validation.EmailValidator();
console.log(validator.isValid("test@example.com"));   // true

Nested Namespaces

namespace App {
    export namespace Models {
        export interface User { id: number; }
    }
}

const user: App.Models.User = { id: 1 };
⚠️ Common Pitfall: For new projects, prefer ES modules (import/export) over namespaces. Namespaces are mostly kept for legacy codebases, global browser scripts without a bundler, and augmenting third-party global types.

ADVANCED9. Module Resolution and CommonJS Interop

TypeScript's moduleResolution setting controls how it locates the files behind an import specifier, and esModuleInterop smooths over differences between ES modules and older CommonJS (Node's original require-based) modules.

// tsconfig.json (relevant excerpt)
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "esModuleInterop": true
  }
}

Importing a CommonJS-Only Package

// Without esModuleInterop, this pattern is often required:
import * as express from "express";

// With esModuleInterop: true, the more familiar default-import
// syntax works even though express itself is CommonJS:
import express from "express";

const app = express();
💡 Tip: The full picture of module-related compiler flags (module, moduleResolution, esModuleInterop, isolatedModules) is covered in depth in the tsconfig guide.

ADVANCED10. Best Practices

1. Prefer Named Exports Over Default Exports

// ✅ Good - consistent names everywhere, easier refactors and auto-imports
export function formatDate(date: Date): string { return date.toISOString(); }

// ❌ Riskier - importer can name it anything, drifting names across files
export default function formatDate(date: Date): string { return date.toISOString(); }

2. Use import type for Type-Only Imports

// ✅ Good - guarantees zero runtime footprint
import type { User } from "./types";

3. Keep Barrel Files Shallow

Deeply nested barrel re-exports (index.ts re-exporting other index.ts files) can slow builds and create circular import issues — keep them to one level where possible.

4. Avoid Namespaces in New Code

// ✅ Good - use ES modules
export interface StringValidator { isValid(s: string): boolean; }

5. Ship or Install Proper Type Declarations

// ✅ Good
// npm install --save-dev @types/lodash

📋 Quick Reference Summary

Concept Key Points
Module Any file with top-level import/export; scoped, not global
Named export/import Multiple per file, explicit names, renamable with as
Default export One per file, imported with any local name
Barrel file Single entry point re-exporting several modules
import type Erased at compile time; guarantees no runtime import
Dynamic import() Async, Promise-based module loading for code splitting
.d.ts files Type-only descriptions of JS code, no runtime output
Namespaces Legacy grouping mechanism; prefer ES modules in new code
